topic_title: Cross-Border Child Custody: What Happens When One Parent Relocates Abroad With a Child
angle: A guide for a parent facing or contemplating an international relocation dispute involving a child — where one NRI parent wants to take a child abroad, or has already done so, without the other parent's consent — explaining how Indian courts approach jurisdiction and the child's best interests, since India is not a party to the Hague Convention on child abduction.
key_points: India is not a signatory to the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, which means there is no automatic, treaty-based mechanism for the swift return of a child brought to or retained in India (or removed from India) in violation of a foreign custody order — each case is decided on its own facts by Indian courts

Indian courts, including the Supreme Court, have developed a 'best interests and welfare of the child' standard for cross-border custody and relocation disputes rather than mechanically enforcing a foreign court's custody order, though a foreign order and the reasons a parent left that jurisdiction are relevant factors the Indian court will weigh

Where a parent has taken a child to India in apparent violation of a foreign custody order, the aggrieved parent can seek a writ of habeas corpus before the relevant Indian High Court, which examines whether the child's continued presence with the parent in India is in the child's best interests, rather than treating the case as a simple contempt of the foreign order

Conversely, a parent in India seeking to relocate abroad with a child (for work, remarriage or family reasons) generally needs either the other parent's consent or a court order permitting relocation, particularly where custody or visitation arrangements are already governed by an Indian court order or a settlement

Given the absence of Hague Convention protection, the most effective safeguard is preventive — a consent order or settlement agreement on custody and travel that explicitly addresses international relocation, passport control, and a clear dispute-resolution mechanism, agreed while both parents are amicable, rather than relying on litigation after a unilateral relocation has already occurred

A parent genuinely concerned about a unilateral cross-border removal should consider requesting the court to direct that both parents' consent (or a specific court order) is needed before either parent can take the child outside India, and should keep the child's passport arrangements documented as part of any custody or visitation order
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: India's non-accession to the 1980 Hague Convention on child abduction: well-settled and widely reported fact, confirmed at research time

Habeas corpus as the primary Indian judicial remedy for cross-border child custody/retention disputes, decided on a best-interests standard: well-settled, confirmed via general family-law practitioner and Supreme Court precedent sources at research time

Preventive consent-order/passport-control safeguards as standard practitioner guidance for cross-border custody risk: general practice guidance, confirmed via general family-law literature at research time

topic_title: Section 29A of the IBC: Who Is Ineligible to Submit a Resolution Plan
angle: A practical guide for prospective resolution applicants, promoters and creditors on the Section 29A ineligibility categories — wilful defaulters, undischarged insolvents, disqualified directors, NPA account holders and connected persons — and how the 'connected person' test and cure periods actually work.
key_points: Section 29A of the IBC bars specified categories of persons from submitting a resolution plan, including undischarged insolvents, wilful defaulters, persons with NPA accounts they haven't cured, persons convicted of certain offences, and disqualified or debarred directors

The 'connected person' concept extends ineligibility beyond the applicant itself to related parties and persons acting jointly or in concert with the applicant, which is frequently where disputes arise
An applicant with an NPA account can cure ineligibility by paying overdue amounts with interest and other charges before submission of the resolution plan
Promoters of the corporate debtor are not automatically barred — the bar turns on whether they fall within one of the specific disqualifying categories, not on their status as promoter alone

The Committee of Creditors and Resolution Professional are required to verify eligibility under Section 29A before a plan is considered, and an ineligible plan cannot be approved even with CoC support

Courts have consistently read Section 29A purposively to keep out those responsible for the corporate debtor's insolvency, while avoiding an overbroad reading that would shrink the pool of genuine bidders
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Section 29A categories and the NPA cure mechanism: well-settled under the IBC as amended, confirmed via standard IBC commentary and case law at research time
Connected person test and purposive judicial interpretation: confirmed via established Supreme Court jurisprudence (e.g., Arcelormittal, Swiss Ribbons lines of authority) at research time

topic_title: Wilful Defaulter Classification: How RBI's 2024 Framework Works and a Borrower's Rights
angle: A guide for a borrower or guarantor facing wilful-defaulter classification, or a lender applying the framework, explaining the identification and review committee process, personal hearing rights and cure options under RBI's Master Direction on Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters.
key_points: RBI's Master Direction on Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters was issued on 30 July 2024 and took effect from 28 October 2024, applying to banks, NBFCs in the middle layer and above, and All-India Financial Institutions
Lenders must examine NPA accounts of Rs. 25 lakh and above for wilful default within six months of the account being classified as NPA

The framework requires a properly constituted identification committee and a separate review committee, and expressly recognises the borrower's and guarantor's right to a personal hearing and to make written submissions before both committees before a final wilful-defaulter classification is made

A show-cause notice must be issued and a written order served by an authorised official before classification is finalised, and lenders' board-approved policies must set out the constitution of these committees and the terms on which compromise settlements with wilful defaulters can be considered

Wilful default carries serious consequences beyond credit blacklisting, including restrictions on raising further finance and potential criminal exposure in appropriate cases, making the personal-hearing stage a critical point for a borrower to contest the classification on facts

The 2024 framework was itself a response to earlier judicial criticism that lenders were classifying borrowers as wilful defaulters without adequate procedural safeguards, and it significantly strengthens those safeguards compared to the pre-2024 position
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Master Direction dated 30 July 2024, effective 28 October 2024: confirmed via azbpartners.com and elplaw.in practitioner summaries at research time
Rs. 25 lakh NPA threshold and 6-month examination window: confirmed via multiple practitioner sources (Lexology, Vinod Kothari) at research time
Identification and review committee structure with personal hearing rights: confirmed via azbpartners.com and metalegal.in summaries at research time

topic_title: Executing a Money Decree in India: The Process Under Order XXI CPC
angle: A practical guide for a decree-holder who has won a money suit but still needs to actually recover the amount, and for a judgment-debtor facing execution proceedings, walking through the Order XXI CPC modes of execution and common obstruction tactics.
key_points: A money decree does not enforce itself — the decree-holder must file a separate execution petition under Order XXI of the Civil Procedure Code, typically before the court that passed the decree or, if assets are elsewhere, a court to which the decree is transferred for execution

Order XXI provides several modes of execution for a money decree, including attachment and sale of the judgment-debtor's movable or immovable property, attachment of salary or bank accounts, and, in limited circumstances, arrest and detention in civil prison
A limitation period of 12 years from the date the decree becomes enforceable generally applies to filing an execution petition, under the Limitation Act, 1963

Judgment-debtors commonly resist execution by filing objections under Section 47 CPC disputing questions relating to execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree, or by claiming exemption for specific categories of property from attachment

Courts have repeatedly emphasised that execution proceedings should not be allowed to become a fresh round of litigation on the merits already decided, and have encouraged executing courts to dispose of execution petitions expeditiously

A decree-holder can also seek execution against a corporate judgment-debtor's directors or officers in limited circumstances, and can combine execution with other statutory recovery routes (such as SARFAESI or IBC, where applicable) depending on the nature of the underlying debt
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Order XXI CPC modes of execution (attachment, sale, arrest/detention) and Section 47 objections: well-settled procedural law under the CPC, confirmed via standard civil procedure commentary at research time
12-year limitation period for execution under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963: well-settled, confirmed at research time

topic_title: PPP Concession Termination: How Compensation Works Under a Model Concession Agreement
angle: A guide for a concessionaire, lender or government authority involved in a PPP infrastructure project (roads, ports, power) facing possible early termination, explaining how Model Concession Agreements structure termination payments differently depending on who is at fault and when termination occurs.
key_points: Model Concession Agreements used for NHAI and other PPP infrastructure projects classify termination into three broad categories: concessionaire default, authority (government) default, and force majeure, each carrying a different compensation formula

Where the concessionaire defaults before the Commercial Operations Date (COD), termination payment is generally tied to physical progress — if progress exceeds a specified threshold (commonly 40% of project cost), a payout applies to the extent of debt due; below that threshold, little or no termination payment is typically due

Where the authority is in material default before COD, compensation typically covers the concessionaire's direct costs and loss of fee or toll revenue, but generally excludes repayment of the concessionaire's debt for that pre-COD period

After COD, authority-default compensation typically shifts to cover interest on debt due and operating and maintenance expenses for the relevant period, reflecting the project's transition to an operating asset

Lenders to PPP projects usually negotiate a direct 'substitution' right allowing them to step in and cure a concessionaire default before termination compensation formulas are triggered, since a termination event significantly affects debt recovery prospects

Disputes over termination payment quantification are a recurring source of arbitration and Section 34 challenges in Indian infrastructure contracts, particularly where a concessionaire relies on a financial-model-based loss-of-profits claim rather than documented, verifiable costs
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: Three-category termination classification (concessionaire default, authority default, force majeure) and COD-linked compensation formulas: confirmed via Nishith Desai Associates and SNR Law practitioner summaries of Model Concession Agreements at research time
40% physical-progress threshold for pre-COD concessionaire-default termination payouts: confirmed via practitioner commentary on amended Model Concession Agreements at research time
Lender substitution rights as a standard PPP financing feature: well-settled market practice, confirmed via practitioner sources at research time

topic_title: Interim Measures Under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act: A Practical Guide Before and During Arbitration
angle: Explain when a party can approach a court for interim relief (injunctions, asset preservation, security) before an arbitral tribunal is even constituted, versus once it exists, and the 'efficacy' test courts apply.
key_points: Section 9 lets a party seek interim measures from a court before, during, or after arbitral proceedings but before enforcement of the award
Once a tribunal is constituted, courts entertain a Section 9 application only if Section 17 relief would not be efficacious
Common reliefs: attachment of assets, injunctions restraining disposal of property, appointment of a receiver, interim custody of goods
Difference between Section 9 (court) and Section 17 (tribunal) interim measures and their enforceability
Limitation and urgency considerations, and interplay with an emergency arbitrator's order
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Section 9 applications lie before, during arbitral proceedings, or after the award but before enforcement under Section 36
confirmed: courts apply CPC Order XXXIX-type principles (prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury) by analogy

topic_title: Multi-Tier Dispute Resolution Clauses: Is Pre-Arbitration Mediation or Negotiation Actually Enforceable?
angle: Practical guide on drafting and enforcing escalation clauses (negotiation -> mediation -> arbitration) common in commercial and infrastructure contracts, and what happens if a party skips a tier.
key_points: Courts generally treat pre-arbitration negotiation/mediation steps as directory rather than a bar to arbitration unless the clause is unambiguous and mandatory
How Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act's mandatory pre-institution mediation interacts with a contractual multi-tier clause
Drafting tips: clear timelines, defined trigger events, and consequences of non-compliance
Risk of a tribunal or court finding a claim premature if a mandatory tier was skipped
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Section 12A Commercial Courts Act mandates pre-institution mediation for commercial suits not seeking urgent interim relief

varies: whether skipping a contractual pre-arbitration tier renders a notice invoking arbitration premature depends on whether the tier is framed as mandatory ('shall') or directory ('may') in the specific clause

topic_title: Invoking a Personal Loan Guarantee: Why a Guarantor's Liability Is Independent of the Borrower's Defences
angle: Distinct from the site's existing bank-guarantee (performance/LC-type) article -- this covers a co-obligant/guarantor's personal liability under a loan guarantee deed under the Indian Contract Act, common in MSME and retail lending.
key_points: Sections 128-140 of the Indian Contract Act: a guarantor's liability is coextensive with the principal debtor's unless the contract says otherwise
Lender need not exhaust remedies against the borrower first before proceeding against the guarantor
Discharge of guarantor: material variance in loan terms without consent, release of security, or lender's own conduct
Guarantor's rights after paying: subrogation to the lender's rights and remedies against the borrower
How a guarantor can be pulled into SARFAESI and IBC Part III personal guarantor proceedings
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Sections 128 and 133-139 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 govern surety liability and discharge
confirmed: Supreme Court has repeatedly held a creditor can proceed against the guarantor without first suing the principal debtor

topic_title: Summary Judgment Under Order XIII-A CPC: When a Commercial Suit Can Skip a Full Trial
angle: Practical guide for businesses on using the summary judgment mechanism unique to the Commercial Courts Act to get a quick decree or dismissal without going through evidence and cross-examination.
key_points: Order XIII-A applies only to commercial disputes under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 and is not available in ordinary civil suits
Either party can apply after summons but before framing of issues, on the ground the other side has no real prospect of succeeding/defending and no other compelling reason for trial
Standard applied: 'no real prospect of success', higher than a demurrer but short of a full trial
What evidence a court will and won't consider at the summary judgment stage
Consequences of an unsuccessful summary judgment application (costs, case management timelines)
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Order XIII-A CPC was introduced by the Commercial Courts, Commercial Division and Commercial Appellate Division of High Courts Act, 2015
confirmed: Delhi High Court has issued practical guidelines clarifying when summary judgment is appropriate in commercial suits (2026)

topic_title: Consumer Mediation Cell: How Pre-Litigation and Court-Referred Mediation Works Under the 2019 Act
angle: Explain the lesser-known mediation route attached to each District/State/National Consumer Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, as an alternative to a full adversarial complaint.
key_points: Every Consumer Commission is required to establish or have access to a Consumer Mediation Cell
Mediation can happen only with consent of both parties, and only after the Commission is satisfied there is a possibility of settlement
Mediation is confidential and settlement terms are recorded and have the same effect as a Commission order
How this differs from the mandatory pre-institution mediation applicable to commercial suits
When mediation is unsuitable (e.g., allegations of fraud or unfair trade practice needing public adjudication)
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Sections 74-81) establishes Consumer Mediation Cells attached to each Commission
confirmed: mediation requires consent of both parties and is referred by the Commission, not automatic

topic_title: Slump Sale vs Asset Sale vs Share Sale: Choosing the Right M&A Structure Under Tax and Company Law
angle: A founder/buyer-facing guide comparing the three common ways to acquire an Indian business, focused on tax treatment, liability transfer, and regulatory approvals for each structure.
key_points: Slump sale (Section 2(42C) Income Tax Act): transfer of an entire undertaking for a lump sum without itemising individual assets/liabilities, taxed as capital gains on net worth
Asset sale: cherry-picking specific assets, each attracting its own stamp duty, GST and transfer formalities; liabilities generally don't transfer unless assumed
Share sale: buyer acquires the target company itself including all liabilities (known and contingent); simpler transfer mechanics (share transfer/demat) but higher diligence stakes
Regulatory triggers: CCI notification thresholds, sectoral FDI approvals, and stamp duty differences across structures
How indemnities and escrow are typically used to bridge the liability-transfer gap between structures
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: 'slump sale' is defined under Section 2(42C) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 as transfer of one or more undertakings for a lump sum consideration without values assigned to individual assets and liabilities
confirmed: capital gains on a slump sale are computed on the 'net worth' of the undertaking under Section 50B

topic_title: Model Standing Orders: When Factories and Large Establishments Must Certify Their Own Standing Orders
angle: A compliance guide for employers on when the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act applies, what Model Standing Orders cover by default, and the process to get establishment-specific standing orders certified.
key_points: Original threshold: applies to industrial establishments with 100 or more workmen (some states/Central Government have reduced this to 50)
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (once in force in a state) raises the standing-orders threshold to 300 workers and consolidates the certification process

Until an employer's own standing orders are certified, the statutory Model Standing Orders apply by default and govern classification of workers, shift timings, leave, termination and disciplinary action
Certification process: draft submission to the Certifying Officer, workman representations, appeal to the appellate authority
Consequences of operating without certified standing orders where the Act applies
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: original threshold under the 1946 Act is 100 or more workmen, with several states and the Central Government having reduced it to 50 by amendment
confirmed: the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 raises the threshold to 300 workers for the standing-orders requirement
varies: exact applicable threshold and whether the Industrial Relations Code is in force depends on the state and its notified rules

topic_title: Health Supplements and Nutraceuticals: FSSAI's Separate Licensing and Claims Regime
angle: A compliance guide for manufacturers of health supplements, nutraceuticals and 'novel foods', which sit under a distinct FSSAI regulation (FSS Health Supplements Regulations, 2016) with different labelling and claims rules than ordinary packaged food.
key_points: The Food Safety and Standards (Health Supplements, Nutraceuticals, Foods for Special Dietary Use, Foods for Special Medical Purpose, Functional Foods and Novel Food) Regulations, 2016 govern this category separately
Products under this category cannot claim to cure, mitigate, treat or prevent disease (that would make them a 'drug')
Specific labelling requirements: recommended dosage, safety warnings, and a mandatory statement that the product is not a substitute for a balanced diet
Product approval/notification process before a new ingredient or health claim can be marketed
Overlap and boundary issues with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act where a product's claims cross into 'drug' territory
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: FSS (Health Supplements, Nutraceuticals...) Regulations, 2016 is the operative regulation for this category, distinct from general packaged food labelling regulations
confirmed: such products are barred from disease prevention/cure/treatment claims under the regulations

topic_title: Bidding in an IBC Liquidation E-Auction: EMD, Forfeiture Risk and What Bidders Must Check Before Paying
angle: A practical guide for prospective bidders in liquidation e-auctions under the IBC, prompted by recent case law upholding forfeiture of amounts well beyond the standard 10% EMD where the auction notice itself provided for it.
key_points: IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 set baseline EMD and process norms (Schedule I) but liquidators can impose stricter auction-specific terms
Courts have held that silence in the Regulations on forfeiture beyond EMD does not protect a defaulting bidder where the auction notice itself has an express forfeiture clause
Practical due diligence: reading the e-auction notice's forfeiture, timeline for balance payment (commonly 90 days), and default consequences before bidding
What happens to sums paid beyond the EMD if the bidder later defaults on the balance sale consideration
Remedies (or lack thereof) for a bidder who wants to challenge forfeiture after the fact
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Supreme Court in M/s ASJ Finsolutions Pvt. Ltd. v. Vikram Bajaj (2026 INSC 1062) upheld forfeiture of an entire deposit beyond the EMD where the e-auction notice expressly so provided
confirmed: Schedule I of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 sets out the standard e-auction process, which liquidators may supplement with stricter terms

topic_title: Force Majeure in Infrastructure and Power Contracts: What Indian Courts Actually Accept
angle: A guide for EPC contractors, concessionaires and power generators on how narrowly Indian courts and tribunals construe force majeure clauses, and what evidence is needed to actually invoke one.
key_points: Force majeure clauses in commercial and infrastructure contracts are construed strictly against the party invoking them -- foreseeable events generally do not qualify
Distinction between a contractual force majeure clause and the doctrine of frustration under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act

What Indian courts/APTEL have accepted or rejected as force majeure in power and EPC disputes (e.g., ordinary regulatory or tax changes typically do not qualify unless specifically listed as a 'change in law' event)
Notice requirements: most contracts require prompt written notice and evidence of mitigation efforts to preserve a force majeure claim
Drafting tips: defining specific triggering events and a clear cap on relief (time extension vs cost compensation)
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: courts and APTEL have held that force majeure clauses in power contracts are construed strictly and those relying on them must show the event was genuinely unforeseeable and beyond their control
confirmed: 'change in law' is typically treated as a separate, specifically defined relief mechanism in PPAs/EPC contracts rather than a subset of force majeure

topic_title: Recording a Trademark or Patent Assignment: The Recordal Process and Why Skipping It Is Risky
angle: Distinct from the site's existing trademark-licensing (registered user agreement) article -- this covers the separate process of recording a change of ownership (assignment) of a trademark or patent with the Registry/Patent Office.
key_points: Difference between a licence (registered user) and an assignment (change of ownership) and why each needs a different Registry filing
Trademark assignment: Form TM-P application, deed of assignment, and the requirement to advertise certain assignments (assignment without goodwill) under Section 42
Patent assignment: Form 16 application to record the assignee as the new patentee, required for the assignee to sue for infringement or enforce the patent

Consequences of an unrecorded assignment: the assignee may be unable to enforce the IP right or claim damages until recordal, and third parties dealing in good faith with the registered owner may prevail
Typical timelines and common defects that cause recordal applications to be objected to
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: trademark assignment is recorded via Form TM-P under the Trade Marks Act, 1999 and Rules, 2017
confirmed: patent assignment is recorded via Form 16 under the Patents Act, 1970 and an unrecorded assignee's ability to sue for infringement can be restricted until recordal

topic_title: When Can an Electricity Dispute Go to Arbitration Instead of the Regulatory Commission? Section 79 Explained
angle: A guide for generators, distribution licensees and their counsel on the boundary between disputes that must go to the regulatory commission (CERC/SERC) under Section 79/86 of the Electricity Act and those that can be arbitrated.
key_points: Section 79(1)(a)-(d) of the Electricity Act, 2003 gives CERC exclusive jurisdiction over specific matters like tariff regulation and inter-state transmission

Tribunal and court rulings have distinguished 'non-tariff' disputes between a generating company and a licensee, which can be referred to arbitration under Section 79(1)(f)/86(1)(f) or a contractual arbitration clause, from tariff-determination disputes which cannot
How a PPA's own arbitration clause interacts with the regulatory commission's jurisdiction
Why getting this characterisation wrong can mean years lost litigating in the wrong forum
Practical drafting guidance for dispute resolution clauses in PPAs and power project contracts
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003 lists CERC's specific regulatory functions in clauses (a) to (f), with clause (f) covering adjudication and referral to arbitration of generator-licensee disputes

confirmed: APTEL has held that non-tariff disputes between a generating company and a distribution licensee can fall outside the regulatory commission's exclusive domain and go to arbitration (subject to ongoing clarification, including a 2026 review ruling)

topic_title: Carpet Area vs Super Built-Up Area Under RERA: What Builders Must Disclose and How to Verify It
angle: A homebuyer-facing guide on RERA's mandatory switch to selling on carpet area, how to independently verify a builder's carpet-area figure, and what to do if the delivered carpet area falls short.
key_points: RERA requires builders to quote and sell on 'carpet area' (defined under Section 2(k)) rather than the older, larger 'super built-up area' that included undivided common area share
How to cross-check the carpet area stated in the Agreement for Sale against the sanctioned building plan filed with the authority
Remedies if the actual carpet area delivered is less than what was disclosed -- refund of the proportionate amount with interest under the RERA Rules
Common builder tactics: bundling balcony/terrace area, or quoting 'saleable area' inconsistently across marketing brochures and the Agreement for Sale
What the RERA registration certificate and project disclosures on the state RERA portal reveal about actual carpet area
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Section 2(k) of RERA, 2016 defines 'carpet area' and requires sale consideration to be based on it
confirmed: RERA Rules require refund of excess amount paid (with interest) if delivered carpet area is less than disclosed, subject to a tolerance threshold prescribed by the state rules

topic_title: Section 73 vs Section 74 (and the New Section 74A) GST Demand Notices: Why the Classification Changes Your Penalty
angle: A practical guide for GST-registered businesses on how to read a demand notice, why the department's choice of section drastically changes penalty exposure and limitation, and how to contest a wrongful Section 74 (fraud) classification.
key_points: Section 73 (no fraud/suppression): 3-year limitation, penalty capped at 10% of tax or Rs. 10,000, nil penalty if paid before SCN
Section 74 (fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression to evade tax): 5-year limitation, penalty escalating up to 100% of tax depending on when payment is made

Section 74A, inserted for periods from FY 2024-25 onwards, merges the two into a common procedure with a unified limitation and graded penalty regardless of fraud allegation, for that prospective period
How to contest a department's use of Section 74 where the underlying facts don't support fraud or suppression, since the extended limitation and higher penalty ride on that classification
Practical steps on receiving a notice: reconciling the demand, responding within timelines, and the effect of voluntary payment before SCN
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Section 73 carries a 3-year limitation and capped 10% penalty (or Rs.10,000, whichever higher) for non-fraud short payment/erroneous refund
confirmed: Section 74 carries a 5-year limitation and up to 100% penalty for fraud/wilful misstatement/suppression cases
confirmed: Section 74A (Finance Act, 2024) applies prospectively from FY 2024-25 onward and unifies the two provisions into a common procedure

topic_title: Can a Non-Farmer Buy Agricultural Land in India? State-by-State Rules Compared
angle: A practical guide comparing how differently Indian states restrict agricultural land purchase by non-agriculturists, since this is a state (not central) subject and the rules vary sharply.
key_points: Land is a State subject, so agricultural land purchase restrictions vary significantly by state tenancy/land-reform legislation

Maharashtra (under the Maharashtra Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948): generally only an 'agriculturist' can buy agricultural land, though holding agricultural land anywhere in India can qualify a buyer

Karnataka: 2020 amendment repealed the old bars (Sections 79A/79B/79C) and the non-farm-income cap, opening agricultural land purchase to non-agriculturists and companies, subject to land ceiling limits
Telangana: permits any Indian citizen to buy agricultural land without an agriculturist certificate or income test, subject to the family ceiling
Land ceiling limits (under state Land Ceiling Acts) continue to cap how much agricultural land any single buyer -- farmer or not -- can hold
Practical due diligence: checking the state's current tenancy/land-reform rules and any recent amendments before structuring a purchase
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Maharashtra restricts agricultural land purchase to 'agriculturists' under the Maharashtra Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, with limited exceptions
confirmed: Karnataka's 2020 amendment opened agricultural land purchase to non-agriculturists by repealing Sections 79A-79C of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act
confirmed: Telangana permits any Indian citizen to purchase agricultural land without an agriculturist certificate
varies: exact rules, ceiling limits and any pending amendments should be checked per state at the time of a specific transaction
